name: presentation-model
intent: Represent the state and behavior of a screen in a model class that does not depend on the GUI framework, so that every display decision and command can be exercised by ordinary unit tests while the view merely projects the model onto the glass.
problem: A screen's dynamic state and behavior live in its widgets: which field is enabled, whether Apply is available, what the title reads. Written as event-handler code next to widget APIs, that logic can only be exercised by driving the real UI, the state is scattered across controls, and every toolkit upgrade or second view - another platform, a test double, a preview - threatens it.
context: Rich-client, mobile and web front-ends whose toolkit separates display from data. It applies when a screen has non-trivial derived state or commands, when the synchronization between model and view can be declared through data binding or written once by hand, and when the team wants unit tests over presentation logic. Fowler's pattern is the framework-independent member of the presentation family (alongside Passive View and Supervising Controller) and is realized by MVVM-style view models in modern toolkits.
benefits: Screen logic becomes ordinary unit-testable code: state, derived enablement and command handlers are plain methods on a model that needs no window, event loop or toolkit object.
The view is reduced to a projection - layout plus binding declarations - so display decisions are made in one place and a rule change touches the model, not every widget.
One model can feed several views (another platform, a preview, a test double), which is why the same element reappears as the ViewModel in WPF, SwiftUI, Compose and Android.
Durable screen state - form contents, current step, selection - can survive view rebuilds such as rotation, re-render or process recreation because it does not belong to any widget.
Presentation policy is encapsulated behind named properties (IsApplyEnabled, IsComposerFieldEnabled) instead of being implicit in widget wiring.
Synchronization can be chosen per project: fine-grained data binding where the framework offers it, coarse-grained save-and-reload where it does not.
tradeoffs: Synchronization is mandatory and repetitive: the model and the view must be kept consistent, and without a binding framework that plumbing is hand-written in both directions - Fowler calls it the most annoying part of the pattern.

Where the synchronization lives is a genuine recurring design cost: in the view it is untested, in the model it couples the model to the view, and a mapper adds another class to an already layered screen.

The presentation model is a second model: duplicating domain rules (validation, totals, business-driven enablement) there creates a second source of truth that drifts, so it must coordinate with the domain layer instead of re-implementing it.
Observers and bindings create lifetime hazards: forgotten disconnects leak the view and keep updating dead widgets, and teardown order can fire handlers against half-destroyed objects.
Writes during change notification can loop or expose transitional state - intermediate values and self-referential bindings are traps the binding frameworks themselves warn about.
Every screen gains a class plus a synchronization mechanism, so trivial screens pay indirection without a payoff, and coarse-grained reload can be wasteful on large screens.

ViewModels tend to accumulate too many responsibilities in practice — inexperienced teams often place all logic (domain rules, orchestration, side effects) into the ViewModel without modularizing, leading to 'god ViewModels' that are hard to test and maintain.
Debugging declarative data bindings is harder than tracing imperative code — binding errors are silent at runtime in many frameworks and can only be detected through careful testing or tooling.
Memory overhead from binding infrastructure and additional observable objects can impact performance on memory-constrained devices when screens are complex.

participants.responsibility: Holds the screen's dynamic state, the derived display decisions and the command handlers, and coordinates with the domain layer; it contains no widget or toolkit types.
Renders the model: lays out widgets, binds their properties to model properties, forwards raw user gestures and command invocations; it makes as few decisions as possible.

Keeps view and model consistent - declarative data binding, observer/listener callbacks or explicit save-and-reload code - and may live in the view, in the model or in a separate mapper (Fowler's placement decision).
Business data and rules that the presentation model reads, validates against and updates; they carry no presentation concerns.
A user-triggered operation exposed by the presentation model together with the predicate that decides when it can run (Apply, Cancel, Save); the view binds a control to it.

use_cases: A data-entry screen whose enablement and visibility rules depend on other fields - the composer field that is editable only while Classical is checked.
Forms with dirty tracking where Apply and Cancel are enabled exactly when the underlying record has changed.
A screen projected by more than one view: desktop and web front-end, phone and tablet, or the real view and a test double.
Mobile screens whose state must survive configuration changes and process death, kept in a ViewModel-backed state holder with saved state.
Wizard and multi-step flows whose current step, validation state and navigation commands are the screen's state.
Test-first development of presentation behavior: drive the model directly and leave only the binding declarations untested.

Cross-platform mobile applications (iOS SwiftUI + Android Jetpack Compose) sharing a common ViewModel/PresentationModel while keeping platform-specific views — Kotlin Multiplatform uses a shared ViewModel that both SwiftUI and Compose observe via KMP-ObservableViewModel.

Offline-first applications where the PresentationModel holds optimistic UI state, pending changes, and sync status separately from the domain model — critical for editors, forms, and content-creation screens.

Screens requiring complex derived state that aggregates multiple domain objects — pricing calculators, dashboard summaries, composite reports — where the aggregation logic belongs in the model, not scattered across widgets.

Enterprise applications with multiple UI technology generations (legacy WPF, modern web, mobile) that must share the same core screen behavior while rendering differently — the PresentationModel is the single source of truth that each view layer consumes.

A WPF or .NET MAUI XAML screen whose controls bind to Presentation Model properties and ICommand/CanExecute commands, keeping save or apply availability out of code-behind while the view remains a projection.

An Android Jetpack Compose screen that obtains a screen-scoped ViewModel, exposes one lifecycle-aware UI state, and retains presentation state across configuration changes while the composable renders it.

A SwiftUI hierarchy where @StateObject owns the observable presentation model and child views receive it through @ObservedObject or bindings, preserving model identity across view updates while keeping rendering declarative.
avoid_when: A purely static screen with no dynamic state and no commands - direct widget code is simpler.
A screen that only mirrors one domain object with no derived state: a direct binding to that object or its DTO is enough.
Trivial confirmations and dialogs where a modal helper function is the whole job.

Immediate-mode interfaces that already rebuild the view from a plain state struct every frame (game GUIs, egui-style tooling): the state struct is the model, and a separate presentation object only adds indirection.
Read-only or generated views where the sync cost dwarfs the screen (a one-shot report page).

Systems requiring complex cross-feature coordination, transactional flows, or global state synchronization at scale — MVVM alone has no opinion on dependency direction, modular boundaries, or orchestration; consider Clean Architecture + Use Cases alongside MVVM for these cases.
anti_patterns: A 'presentation model' that holds widget or toolkit objects and pokes them directly — the logic remains untestable and the model is coupled to one view.
Re-implementing domain rules (validation, pricing, permissions) inside the presentation model so the rule now exists twice and drifts apart from the domain layer.
A global or singleton screen-state object that any part of the program may mutate, undermining the one-model-per-screen discipline.
Code-behind handlers that keep doing the presentation work while a presentation-model class exists in name only.
Listeners, bindings or observers that are never detached when the view closes, so dead views keep receiving updates.
Fine-grained property notifications that fire on every intermediate value of a computation, provoking redundant or oscillating updates.

The 'God ViewModel': a single ViewModel that accumulates API calls, business logic, orchestration, side effects (navigation, analytics, permissions), and UI state — resulting in 800–1500 line files that are hard to test, debug, and maintain. Fix: introduce a domain/use-case layer to handle orchestration, keeping the ViewModel as a thin UI state coordinator.

Direct API calls from the ViewModel without a repository abstraction — couples the ViewModel to the network layer, breaks testability, and violates the dependency inversion principle. Fix: inject repositories that abstract data sources (API, DB, cache).

Exposing raw API models directly to the UI — couples the UI to backend schema, so any API change breaks the view. Fix: map to UI state models (preferably sealed classes or state holders) inside the ViewModel.

Multiple independent LiveData/StateFlow variables for what is conceptually one UI state (loading + data + error as separate observables) — creates implicit invalid state combinations and makes the UI state hard to reason about. Fix: model UI state as a single sealed class or discriminated union (e.g., ContentState<Loading | Loaded | Error>) with a deterministic reducer.

Leaking Android Context or other lifecycle-aware objects into the ViewModel — causes memory leaks when the ViewModel outlives the Activity. ViewModels must not hold references to Context or any lifecycle-bound object.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: presentation decisions live apart from rendering and widget mechanics.
Single responsibility: one presentation model for one view (or child control), deciding what to display, not how it is drawn.
Dependency inversion: the view depends on the model, and the model depends on domain abstractions — never on the toolkit.
Information hiding: named model properties such as IsApplyEnabled encapsulate how a display decision is made.
Humble object and testability: keep the untestable part (the view) as dumb as possible and move decisions where tests can reach them.
No duplicated domain logic: the model coordinates with domain objects, it does not restate their rules.
Composition over growing one screen-wide object: child PresentationModels should be composed rather than merged into a monolithic screen class.
State as a single source of truth: model all UI state for a screen in one sealed state class rather than multiple independent observables that can form invalid combinations.
ViewModel as a coordinator, not a container: business logic and orchestration belong in domain use cases, not in the ViewModel.
Synchronization strategy must be explicit: decide and document whether binding, observer callbacks, or save-and-reload is authoritative for each data flow direction.
best_practices: Keep toolkit types out of the model (except the narrow listener interface it owns); if the model must reference the view, keep that interface small and stubbable for testing.
Expose derived state as read-only properties rather than letting the view compute enablement or visibility — the model knows why a field is disabled, the view just needs the boolean.
Use the framework's binding where it exists and hand-write coarse-grained save-and-reload where it does not; state which direction is authoritative for each binding.

Detach observers and bindings on view teardown, or use the framework's automatic or weak connection facility where it has one — forgotten subscriptions are the leading cause of memory leaks in MVVM applications.
Keep getters and setters trivial wherever binding tracks dependencies: compute into locals and assign once so dependent properties never observe intermediate values.
Test the model without the UI; if you feel compelled to test the view's synchronization, first check whether logic leaked out of the model.
Keep one presentation model per view or child control; compose child models instead of growing one screen-wide god object.

Expose UI state as a single sealed state class (e.g., Loading | Content(data) | Error(msg)) rather than multiple independent observables — this makes illegal states unrepresentable and simplifies UI rendering logic.

Do not place business logic in the ViewModel — delegate to domain use cases or repositories. The ViewModel coordinates; the domain layer executes. This separation is what allows the ViewModel to stay thin and testable.
Use lifecycle-aware scopes (viewModelScope in Android, @StateObject in SwiftUI) for all async work in the ViewModel, ensuring work is cancelled when the screen is destroyed.

In Kotlin Multiplatform, use KMP-ObservableViewModel with @NativeCoroutinesState to share a ViewModel between SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose; export lifecycle-viewmodel to the iOS binary framework to avoid runtime compatibility issues.
Prefer immutable state objects with copy() (Kotlin data classes) or with() (Swift structs) when updating — immutable updates prevent subtle state corruption bugs in concurrent scenarios.

Prefer StateFlow over LiveData in Kotlin for new code (Flow is part of the Kotlin standard library, composes better with coroutines, and is available in Kotlin Multiplatform), and prefer @Published over manual property observation in SwiftUI.
Use sealed classes for UI state modeling in Jetpack Compose and SwiftUI; the compiler enforces exhaustive switch handling, preventing forgotten states.

When using data binding in WPF/Xamarin/.NET MAUI, prefer one-way bindings by default and only introduce two-way bindings intentionally — unexpected two-way updates are a common source of oscillation bugs.

In Jetpack Compose, treat the ViewModel as the single source of truth for UI state, expose state via StateFlow, and use collectAsStateWithLifecycle() in composables to properly respect the lifecycle owner.

related_patterns_notes.model-view-presenter: MVP is the broader family that Presentation Model belongs to. In MVP, the Presenter typically holds state and coordinates view updates through an interface. Presentation Model differs in that it abstracts the entire view as a model class without requiring the presenter to reference a concrete view interface. The key distinction: Presentation Model owns all view state directly, while MVP typically separates state (in the Model) from presentation logic (in the Presenter). MVP tends to couple the presenter to the view through an interface; Presentation Model achieves looser coupling through data binding rather than explicit presenter-to-view calls.
related_patterns_notes.model-view-viewmodel: MVVM is a framework-specific realization of Presentation Model, popularized by Microsoft's WPF and Silverlight. The ViewModel IS the Presentation Model. MVVM makes the pattern concrete by relying on a declarative binding layer (XAML data binding) to handle synchronization automatically, whereas Fowler's original Presentation Model left the synchronization strategy as an explicit design decision. Modern frameworks (SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, Angular, Vue with Composition API) all implement MVVM-style ViewModels. The 2025 multivocal literature review (Fuksa et al.) identifies 76 additional design constructs and 29 design aspects beyond the standard MVVM definition, showing how deeply the pattern has evolved.
related_patterns_notes.model-view-intent: MVI (Model-View-Intent) builds on MVVM's unidirectional data flow but adds explicit state machines for screen state, making illegal states unrepresentable. Where MVVM exposes mutable observable properties (potentially allowing invalid state combinations like loading=true + error!=null simultaneously), MVI uses sealed state classes with deterministic reducers. MVI is particularly relevant in declarative UI frameworks (Jetpack Compose, SwiftUI) where the UI is a pure function of state. MVI does not replace MVVM; it constrains how the ViewModel's state is modeled to prevent implicit state relationships from becoming bugs.
related_patterns_notes.flux-redux: Flux and Redux (global state containers) differ from Presentation Model in scope and intent. Presentation Model addresses per-screen state and logic; Redux addresses global application state shared across screens. Redux uses a single store with pure reducers (unidirectional data flow), while Presentation Model uses per-screen ViewModels with two-way binding support. In practice, MVVM often combines with Redux-pattern libraries (e.g., NgRx in Angular, Zustand, MobX) to handle global cross-screen state, while each screen's PresentationModel/ViewModel handles local screen state. The relationship is complementary: Redux manages app-wide state, Presentation Model manages screen-level state. Flux/Redux have no built-in concept of screen lifecycle or configuration-change survival, whereas the ViewModel in Android, or @StateObject in SwiftUI, does.
related_patterns_notes.humble-object: The View in Presentation Model is intentionally made a Humble Object — it contains almost no logic, delegating all decisions to the Presentation Model. This is the primary testability mechanism: the untestable widget wiring stays in the view, which is either not tested at all or tested through integration tests, while all meaningful logic resides in the highly testable Presentation Model. The pattern deliberately inverts the typical GUI structure where the view is intelligent and domain logic leaks into event handlers.
related_patterns_notes.observer: The synchronization mechanism in Presentation Model is fundamentally Observer (or PropertyChangeNotifier). The Presentation Model fires property-change events; the View subscribes and updates widgets accordingly. Modern frameworks encode this differently — INotifyPropertyChanged in .NET, @Published in Swift, StateFlow/MutableStateFlow in Kotlin, @Observable in Vue — but the pattern is the same. Fowler notes that fine-grained property change notifications can create oscillation and performance problems; coarser notifications (per-field or per-command) are safer.
related_patterns_notes.presentational-vs-container: React's distinction between Presentational and Container Components maps closely to Presentation Model. Container components (like ViewModels) handle data fetching, state management, and business logic; Presentational components handle rendering. This separation is identical to Fowler's intent, though React's model is less formal. React hooks (useState, useReducer, useContext) can implement Presentation Model patterns, and libraries like Recoil, Jotai, and Zustand provide state primitives that serve similar roles to a Presentation Model in a React context.
related_patterns_notes.supervising-controller: Supervising Controller is a sibling pattern in Fowler's presentation family. It differs from Presentation Model in where state lives: Supervising Controller stores UI state in the View (with simple display logic handled declaratively through binding), and the Presenter handles complex logic. Presentation Model stores all state in the Presentation Model, making it more testable but requiring explicit synchronization. The tradeoff: Presentation Model supports multiple views of the same state more naturally, while Supervising Controller is lighter-weight when only one view exists.
related_patterns_notes.passive-view: Passive View is the extreme end of the presentation family where the View has zero logic — it is purely a canvas for widget instantiation. All state and logic lives in the Presenter. Presentation Model is less extreme: the View may hold synchronization logic (in the 'model references view' variant), and the Presentation Model may own some view-interface responsibilities. Passive View achieves maximum testability but demands more code to synchronize; Presentation Model trades a small amount of testability for less synchronization boilerplate.
related_patterns_notes.clean-architecture: Presentation Model operates at the UI layer of Clean Architecture. The Presentation Model is the 'driving adapter' that coordinates use cases and entities. Clean Architecture's Use Cases define orchestration boundaries that prevent the Presentation Model from becoming a 'god object' that accumulates all business logic. The 2026 'Why MVVM Is Not Enough' analysis (Ivantsov) shows that fat ViewModels are a structural consequence of missing use-case/orchestration boundaries, not a discipline failure — making Clean Architecture's layering a necessary complement to Presentation Model in complex systems.
